| CO | **Ni single-atom catalysts (Ni SACs)** | Ni SACs delivered **current densities >100 mA cm^-2** with **nearly 100% FE(CO)**; in a **10 × 10 cm^2** modular cell they produced **3.34 L h^-1 CO** at **>8 A** overall current while remaining nearly exclusively CO-selective (zheng2019largescaleandhighly pages 1-3) | Isolated Ni sites on carbon favor CO2-to-CO while suppressing HER, giving very high CO selectivity on a non-noble, scalable platform (zheng2019largescaleandhighly pages 1-3) | Important counterexample to Cu-centered thinking: for **CO**, atomically dispersed Ni can outperform Cu decisively in selectivity and scale; some Ni systems are less cation-sensitive than Ag, underscoring catalyst-specific electrolyte effects (zheng2019largescaleandhighly pages 1-3, kim2022theinsensitivecation pages 6-8) |
| Formate | **Bi-based catalysts (nanosheets, dendrites, nanotubes, flow-cell Bi)** | Ultrathin Bi nanosheets reported **~100% FE(formate)** over a broad potential window; exfoliated ultrathin Bi nanosheets gave **86% FE** at **16.5 mA cm^-2**; Bi from BiOI gave **>90% FE** and **24 mA cm^-2**; electrodeposited Bi dendrites reached **96.4% FE** and **14.6 mA cm^-2**; flow-cell Bi catalysts sustained **>90% FE** up to **200 mA cm^-2**, and defective Bi nanotubes delivered **~288 mA cm^-2** (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6, hoffman2019highselectivitytowards pages 1-2, han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11) | Main-group Bi stabilizes the *OCHO pathway and suppresses competing H2 / CO formation, making Bi highly selective for formate rather than multicarbon products (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6, han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11) | Performance depends strongly on reactor design: H-cells are often limited to **<30 mA cm^-2** formate partial current because of CO2 transport, whereas GDE / flow architectures unlock industrially relevant rates (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6, han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11) |
| Formate | **In-based catalysts** | Bulk/porous/anodized In catalysts reported **~90–100% FE(formate)** in several cases: bulk In about **95% FE** at **5 mA cm^-2**; hp-In about **90% FE** at **67.5 mA cm^-2**; sulfur-doped In **95% FE** at **58.9 mA cm^-2**; some In0–In2O3 composites were reported near **100% FE** (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6, han2020promisesofmain pages 6-8, han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11) | In-based materials favor formate formation and can achieve high rates / selectivities inaccessible to typical Cu for this product class (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6, han2020promisesofmain pages 6-8, han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11) | Oxide state and morphology can matter, but the key comparison is product-specific: In is far better than Cu when the desired product is formate, not C2+ (han2020promisesofmain pages 6-8, han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11) |
| Formate | **Sn-based catalysts** | Representative Sn entries include nano-SnO2/graphene at **93.6% FE** and **9.5 mA cm^-2**; Sn(S)/Au at **93% FE** and **51.1 mA cm^-2**; mesoporous SnO2-derived catalysts about **87% FE** with **~45 mA cm^-2** partial current; SnOx nanoparticles often in the **~80–90% FE** range (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6, han2020promisesofmain pages 6-8, hoffman2019highselectivitytowards pages 1-2) | Sn / SnOx surfaces promote the formate pathway, though oxide thickness and precursor state affect activity and FE (han2020promisesofmain pages 6-8) | Native SnOx can improve selectivity yet sometimes reduce overall current; another example that oxidation state effects can be beneficial or detrimental depending on thickness / precursor evolution (han2020promisesofmain pages 6-8) |


*Table: This table compares copper and leading alternative electrocatalysts across the main CO2RR product classes: C2+ products, CO, and formate. It highlights where Cu remains distinctive and where Au, Ag, Ni single atoms, Bi, In, and Sn outperform it, while also flagging major sources of contradictory selectivity findings.*

### When copper is “best”

**Cu is the standout choice if the target is multicarbon (C2+) products** (ethylene, ethanol, etc.), because other common metals either (i) stop at CO (Au/Ag/Zn-like) or (ii) favor formate (Sn/Bi/In-like) or (iii) favor H2 because of strong CO poisoning (Pt/Ni/Fe-like), whereas Cu can further reduce *CO toward hydrocarbons/alcohols (gattrell2006areviewof pages 1-2, todorova2019mechanisticunderstandingof pages 1-3). Modern Cu catalysts with engineered steps/defects can reach high ethylene selectivity (e.g., ethylene FE >70% reported for stepped Cu nanowires with long stability) (choi2020highlyactiveand pages 1-2), while classic single-crystal work shows facet control can shift selectivity dramatically (Cu(100) favoring C2H4 versus Cu(111) favoring CH4; stepped surfaces boosting C2H4/CH4 ratios) (hori2002selectiveformationof pages 1-2, hori2002selectiveformationof media 85137206).

### Where alternatives outperform copper

**CO production (syngas feedstock): Au/Ag and Ni single-atom catalysts outperform Cu on selectivity and product simplicity.**

* Au gas diffusion electrodes can deliver **80–90% CO FE** at **up to 200 mA cm−2** in acidic sulfate electrolytes, with only CO and H2 detected, and improved process energy efficiency relative to neutral operation (monteiro2021efficiencyandselectivity pages 1-3).
* Engineered Ag/Au systems can combine high selectivity and high rate: Au adparticles on Ag in an MEA sustained **>90% CO FE** to ~**240 mA cm−2** and showed multi‑tens of hours stability (ozden2021goldadparticleson pages 10-18).
* Non‑noble **Ni single‑atom catalysts** can reach **>100 mA cm−2** with **nearly 100% CO Faradaic selectivity**, including scaled operation (>8 A current in a 10×10 cm2 modular cell) (zheng2019largescaleandhighly pages 1-3).

**Formate production: Bi/Sn/In (main-group) catalysts outperform Cu on selectivity.**

Bi- and In-based catalysts are repeatedly reported with **>90% to ~100% formate FE** (including flow configurations reaching large currents, e.g., >90% FE at 200 mA cm−2 for some Bi systems) (han2020promisesofmain pages 10-11). Reviews compiling many systems show numerous Sn/Bi/In catalysts with very high FE and substantial partial current densities, including architectures that exceed what is typically feasible in H-cells (transport limited) (han2020promisesofmain pages 5-6).

## Contradictory findings about CO2RR selectivity (what disagrees, and why)

### 1) What is the “active state” of oxide-derived copper (Cu+, subsurface O, or fully reduced Cu0)?

A central controversy is whether high C2+ selectivity on oxide-/hydroxide-derived Cu arises from **persisting Cu+ / subsurface oxygen** motifs versus primarily **metallic Cu0 surfaces that have been restructured**.

* Evidence emphasizing oxidation state: some studies argue Cu+ and/or subsurface oxygen (and oxygen vacancies) reduce CO2 activation barriers and promote downstream C–C coupling, while Cu2+-like oxides can be inactive due to carbonate passivation layers (velascovelez2018theroleof pages 9-12, velascovelez2018theroleof pages 12-15).
* Evidence emphasizing reduction/restructuring: other studies report oxide-/hydroxide-derived electrodes are **reduced to Cu0 at steady state**; enhanced C2+ selectivity is then attributed to **fragmentation into nanosized grains**, extensive **grain boundaries**, and exposure of **high-index facets**, rather than a stable Cu+ state (lei2020investigatingtheorigin pages 1-2).

These contradictory assignments are plausibly reconciled by the fact that oxide-derived Cu evolves dynamically under cathodic potentials: preparation history, timescale, and probe sensitivity can yield different apparent “states,” while the real active surface may be a mixed, reconstructed ensemble (Cu0 with defects and possibly trapped subsurface O) (zheng2019understandingtheroadmap pages 5-6, todorova2019mechanisticunderstandingof pages 10-11).

### 2) Surface structure contradictions: terraces vs steps vs reconstruction

Single-crystal work shows selectivity depends strongly on facet/step structure (e.g., Cu(111) mainly CH4 vs Cu(100) more C2H4; stepped Cu can strongly raise C2H4/CH4 ratios) (hori2002selectiveformationof pages 1-2, hori2002selectiveformationof media 85137206). Yet later mechanistic discussions highlight disagreement over whether **pristine Cu(100) terraces** or **stepped/high-index sites** (and/or reconstruction-generated motifs) are the key C2H4-active sites, because Cu surfaces can reconstruct during CO2RR (zheng2019understandingtheroadmap pages 5-6). This creates genuine contradictions when different studies use different pre-treatments, potentials, or operando windows.

### 3) Electrolyte cation effects: from “rate/selectivity tuning” to “no CO2RR without cations”

Cation effects are not merely quantitative; they can be qualitative.

* In highly controlled experiments at pH 3, CO2RR on Au/Ag/Cu was reported to be **absent without metal cations** (“CO is only produced … if a metal cation is added”), with activity restored by adding trace alkali cations (monteiro2021absenceofco2 pages 1-2).
* Other studies show strong cation dependence in practical cells (e.g., Li+ leading to nearly no CO on Au GDEs under some conditions; Cs+ markedly promoting CO formation) (monteiro2021efficiencyandselectivity pages 3-4).

Thus, contradictory selectivity observations across laboratories can arise simply because different electrolytes (cation identity/concentration) change the interfacial electric field and stabilization of key intermediates (monteiro2021absenceofco2 pages 2-3).

### 4) Local pH/buffering and mass transport: shifting CO vs H2 and C2 vs C1

CO2RR selectivity on Cu is sensitive to electrolyte/buffering and local pH, consistent with early observations that Cu product selectivity is electrolyte- and pH-dependent (hori1990formationofhydrocarbons pages 1-2). Reviews emphasize that weak buffers and high local pH can favor C2 products, while stronger buffers can shift selectivity toward CH4/H2; these effects scale with current density and reactor design because proton consumption and CO2 depletion are transport-coupled (zheng2019understandingtheroadmap pages 4-5).

## Summary statement

Copper is best viewed as the **benchmark (and often the only broadly effective pure metal) for C2+ CO2RR**, but it is **not** the best general CO2RR catalyst across products: for **CO**, Au/Ag (and especially optimized Au–Ag structures and Ni single-atom catalysts) can achieve higher CO selectivity at industrial current densities; for **formate**, Bi/Sn/In systems can reach near-unity formate selectivity and high rates. Much of the apparent disagreement in the literature about “selectivity” stems from genuine, reproducible sensitivity to catalyst state (oxide-derived vs reduced), dynamic restructuring, and electrochemical environment (cations, buffering, mass transport, and cell architecture) (zheng2019largescaleandhighly pages 1-3, lei2020investigatingtheorigin pages 1-2, monteiro2021absenceofco2 pages 1-2, zheng2019understandingtheroadmap pages 4-5).

### Performance Assessment and Selectivity Contradictions in CO2 Electrocatalysts

**1. Introduction.** The electrochemical CO2 reduction reaction (CO2RR) converts greenhouse gas into fuels and feedstocks. Copper (Cu) has long been considered unique as the only monometallic material capable of producing significant multi-carbon (C2+) hydrocarbons and alcohols (ethylene, ethanol). However, the "best" catalyst depends on the target product and operating environment, as alternatives frequently outperform copper for single-carbon (C1) pathways.

**2. Copper vs. Alternative Electrocatalysts.** CO synthesis: gold (Au) and silver (Ag) are highly selective for CO (FE often >80%); nickel single-atom catalysts (Ni SACs) achieve high CO selectivity while suppressing HER. Formate synthesis: bismuth (Bi) and tin (Sn) significantly outperform copper for formate (Bi FEs of 92–94.1%), especially in bimetallic Bi-Cu structures. Advanced multi-carbon targets: nickel phosphides and Ni-Ga alloys can bypass scaling relations, with nickel phosphides reducing CO2 to C3/C4 liquids at overpotentials as low as 10 mV.

**3. Contradictory Findings in CO2 Reduction Selectivity.** Active oxidation state (Cu0 vs. Cu+): one school asserts oxides are unstable at CO2RR potentials and reduce to Cu0, attributing selectivity to residual surface defects; others argue stabilized Cu+ sites or subsurface oxygen are essential for C-C coupling. Subsurface oxygen stability: some operando studies suggest oxygen remains and withdraws electron density, while high-temporal-resolution mass spectrometry concludes oxide reduction precedes product formation. Facet vs. defect dependency: the accepted view is Cu(100) favors ethylene and Cu(111) favors methane, but recent findings suggest pristine ordered facets favor hydrogen and that steps/defects formed during pretreatment are the actual C2H4 sites. The cation effect: many believe larger cations (Cs+) enhance CO2RR by buffering interfacial pH, but in-situ spectroscopy shows interfacial CO2 concentration decreases with cation size, implying selectivity is driven by CO2 depletion rate rather than buffering.

**4. Conclusion.** Copper is not the best electrocatalyst for all CO2 reduction pathways, but it remains the most effective monometallic catalyst for multi-carbon products. For C1 conversions, bismuth, gold, and nickel-based materials provide superior selectivity and lower overpotentials. The field still grapples with contradictions about active oxidation state and facet-vs-defect roles.

question: Do solid-state electrolytes solve the safety problems of lithium batteries, or introduce new ones? What conflicting results exist about electrolyte stability?

alone.answer:
Solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) **reduce several major safety risks of conventional Li-ion cells, but they do not make Li batteries intrinsically safe**. They also introduce different failure modes whose severity depends strongly on SSE chemistry, interfaces, pressure, current density, and state of charge.

## What safety problems they help solve

- **Less flammable electrolyte inventory:** Oxide and many sulfide ceramics do not burn like carbonate solvents. This reduces vapor ignition, leakage, and separator-shutdown/melting issues.
- **Better high-temperature dimensional stability:** Ceramic SSEs do not shrink like polyolefin separators.
- **Potentially less gas/fire in abuse:** In some nail/thermal-abuse scenarios, all-solid cells can release less flammable gas than liquid-electrolyte cells, but this is not universal.

## New or remaining safety problems

1. **Lithium metal shorting is still possible**
   - Li can grow as filaments through pores, grain boundaries, cracks, or along interfaces, especially under high local current density or poor contact.
   - “High shear modulus stops dendrites” is too simple; brittle fracture, defects, and current focusing dominate.
   - Key examples: Porz et al. showed Li penetration through garnet-type ceramics via defects/grain boundaries, *Adv. Energy Mater.* 2017, DOI: **10.1002/aenm.201701003**. Kasemchainan et al. showed stripping-induced voids and current constriction can trigger later Li penetration, *Nat. Mater.* 2019, DOI: **10.1038/s41563-019-0438-9**.

2. **Thermal runaway can still occur**
   - The cathode and lithiated anode remain chemically energetic. Charged Ni-rich layered oxides can release oxygen/heat; Li metal reacts violently with many decomposition products.
   - Removing liquid electrolyte removes one fuel, but not the stored electrochemical energy.

3. **Sulfide SSEs introduce toxic/moisture hazards**
   - Li₂S–P₂S₅-based glasses, LGPS-type materials, and argyrodites such as Li₆PS₅Cl can hydrolyze to **H₂S**, a toxic gas.
   - They also tend to oxidize at high-voltage cathodes and reduce at Li metal unless protected.

4. **Interfaces can be chemically unstable**
   - Interphases may be beneficial if electronically insulating/passivating, or dangerous if mixed-conducting and continuously growing.
   - Stack pressure, particle cracking, and cathode volume change can break passivation and create hot spots.

5. **Polymer “solid” electrolytes are a different case**
   - Many polymer or gel-polymer electrolytes still contain flammable organic components and may soften at moderate temperatures. They do not solve fire risk to the same extent as dense ceramics.

---

## Conflicting results on electrolyte stability

A major conflict in the field is that many SSEs were initially reported to have **very wide electrochemical stability windows**, often 0–5 or 0–6 V vs Li/Li⁺, while thermodynamic calculations and later interfacial spectroscopy show much narrower intrinsic stability.

### 1. LGPS and sulfide electrolytes

**Optimistic result:**  
LGPS, Li₁₀GeP₂S₁₂, was reported as a superionic conductor with apparent high-voltage compatibility; original landmark report: Kamaya et al., *Nat. Mater.* 2011, DOI: **10.1038/nmat3066**.

**Conflicting result:**  
First-principles work predicted that LGPS is thermodynamically stable only in a narrow window, roughly around **1.7–2.1 V vs Li/Li⁺**, decomposing against Li metal to Li₂S, Li₃P, Li–Ge alloys, etc., and oxidizing at high voltage. Mo, Ong and Ceder, *Chem. Mater.* 2012, DOI: **10.1021/cm203303y**.

**Resolution:**  
LGPS may look stable in slow voltammetry or in cells with poor electronic contact because decomposition products passivate or because electron transfer is kinetically limited. In composite cathodes with carbon, intimate contact, and high surface area, sulfide oxidation is much more evident.

### 2. “Wide electrochemical windows” from linear sweep voltammetry

**Optimistic result:**  
Many oxides and sulfides show little current up to 5–6 V in LSV/CV when tested with blocking electrodes.

**Conflicting result:**  
DFT phase-equilibrium studies predict that most SSEs are not intrinsically stable over the full 0–5 V Li-battery range. See Richards et al., *Chem. Mater.* 2016, DOI: **10.1021/acs.chemmater.5b04082**.

**Resolution:**  
LSV often measures kinetic/electronic limitations, not true thermodynamic stability. If the SSE is electronically insulating, decomposition currents can be tiny even when the reaction is thermodynamically favorable. Adding carbon improves electron access but can also exaggerate practical decomposition relative to a real dense interface.

### 3. Sulfide cathode interfaces: stable vs unstable

**Optimistic result:**  
High-energy all-solid-state cells using sulfide electrolytes and coated cathodes have shown good cycling, e.g. Kato et al. with high-power sulfide-based cells, *Nat. Energy* 2016, DOI: **10.1038/nenergy.2016.30**.

**Conflicting result:**  
Uncoated sulfide/cathode interfaces often react chemically or electrochemically with layered oxides such as LiCoO₂ or NMC, forming resistive interphases and causing impedance growth.

**Resolution:**  
Cathode coatings such as LiNbO₃, Li₂ZrO₃, LiTaO₃, or Li₃PO₄ can suppress direct sulfide oxidation and interdiffusion. Thus the electrolyte may be unstable intrinsically but usable with interfacial engineering.

### 4. Garnet LLZO: stable against Li or not?

**Optimistic result:**  
Garnet oxides such as Li₇La₃Zr₂O₁₂, LLZO, are often described as among the most Li-metal-compatible SSEs.

**Conflicting result:**  
Thermodynamic calculations suggest LLZO is not perfectly stable at 0 V vs Li/Li⁺; reduction and interphase formation are possible. High-voltage oxidation is also thermodynamically possible.

**Resolution:**  
LLZO is often **kinetically stable enough** against Li because decomposition products can be thin and passivating. However, surface Li₂CO₃/LiOH contamination, dopants such as Al/Ta/Ga, grain boundaries, and mechanical flaws can dominate observed behavior.

### 5. LiPON: unusually stable in practice, but not necessarily thermodynamically inert

LiPON thin-film electrolyte works well with Li metal because it forms a stable, electronically insulating interphase. This is practical stability, not necessarily a claim that no decomposition occurs. Classic thin-film battery work: Bates et al., *Solid State Ionics* 2000, DOI: **10.1016/S0167-2738(00)00327-1**.

---

## Bottom line

Solid-state electrolytes **mitigate flammable-liquid and separator-related hazards**, but they **do not eliminate battery safety risk**. The main new risks are Li-metal penetration, brittle fracture, interfacial decomposition, sulfide moisture toxicity, and persistent thermal runaway from energetic electrodes.

The apparent contradictions in electrolyte stability mostly come from mixing up:

- **Thermodynamic stability**: is decomposition favorable?
- **Kinetic stability**: is electron/ion transfer slow enough to prevent it?
- **Interphase passivation**: does the decomposition stop itself?
- **Test geometry artifacts**: blocking electrodes, carbon additives, poor contact, pressure, and surface contamination.

So the correct view is: many SSEs are **not intrinsically stable over the full Li-battery voltage range**, but some can be **practically stable** if the interphase is passivating or engineered with coatings/interlayers.

unified.answer:
**Bottom line:** Solid-state electrolytes **address major liquid-electrolyte hazards**—especially flammability, volatilization, and leakage—but they **do not eliminate battery safety problems**. They shift the safety problem toward **lithium filament/dendrite penetration, defect-driven failure, interfacial instability, and—in sulfide electrolytes—moisture-triggered H₂S generation**.

### What safety problems they can solve
Several papers frame inorganic or solid electrolytes as safer than organic liquid electrolytes because they avoid flammable liquid components, volatilization, and leakage, while potentially enabling wider voltage windows and higher energy density (10.1016/j.ensm.2019.08.029; 10.3791/56259; 10.1002/eem2.12670; 10.1002/adfm.202412548). Replacing flammable liquids with solid polymer electrolytes is likewise described as a promising route to safer Li-metal batteries (10.1016/j.mtener.2020.100522).

### What new or unresolved safety problems they introduce
The strongest counterpoint is that solid electrolytes can still be penetrated by lithium. Multiple studies identify **Li dendrite/filament penetration through solid-state electrolytes** as a major safety and rate-performance constraint (10.1002/adfm.202000831; 10.1016/J.ENSM.2019.03.004; 10.1002/aenm.202102148; 10.1002/aenm.202102825). Direct observation of Li dendrites inside garnet electrolytes was reported, explicitly questioning whether solid electrolytes reliably prevent dendrite growth (10.1039/C6TA05439K). Dendrite growth has also been reported in SSE pellets, with Li penetrating through grain boundaries and being reduced to metallic Li inside garnet pellets (10.1016/j.chempr.2020.06.030).

A key nuance is that **mechanical stiffness alone is not a guaranteed solution**. The Monroe–Newman criterion suggested an electrolyte shear modulus at least twice that of Li metal should suppress dendrites, but high-modulus garnet electrolytes have still been penetrated through grain boundaries above 0.5 mA cm⁻² (10.1016/J.CHEMPR.2018.11.013). Other work found Li penetration depends more on **defect size and density** than on shear modulus or surface roughness (10.1016/J.JOULE.2018.06.021; 10.1016/J.JOULE.2018.07.009). Thus, the literature conflicts with a simple “hard solid stops dendrites” view: some claims emphasize mechanical strength as necessary (10.3389/fmats.2020.00111), while others show defects, cracks, pores, and grain boundaries can dominate failure (10.1016/J.JOULE.2018.07.009).

Sulfide solid electrolytes add another safety issue: **moisture sensitivity and H₂S formation**. Several papers state that sulfides hydrolyze or react with moisture, generating toxic H₂S gas (10.1038/s41565-020-0657-x; 10.3389/fenrg.2014.00025; 10.1016/J.JOULE.2018.07.028; 10.1016/J.CHEMPR.2018.11.013). This is a new hazard relative to the claimed benefits of eliminating flammable liquids.

### Conflicting results on electrolyte stability
There is a clear tension in the evidence:

- **Broad solid-state claims:** all-solid-state batteries are described as having higher stability, no leakage, and wider voltage windows than liquid-electrolyte cells (10.1016/j.ensm.2019.08.029).
- **Sulfide-specific limitations:** sulfide electrolytes are reported to suffer from moisture sensitivity, narrow intrinsic electrochemical windows, side reactions with electrodes, poor solid–solid contact, and interfacial instability (10.1016/j.jmat.2020.09.003; 10.1002/aenm.202402929; 10.1016/j.electacta.2019.134943; 10.1002/adfm.202305373).

There are also stabilizing modifications that complicate the picture. Chlorine substitution in sulfide electrolytes is reported to inhibit Li dendrite penetration and suppress bulk/interfacial decomposition by enhancing voltage stability (10.1016/j.ensm.2021.12.008). A modified sulfide glass-ceramic electrolyte showed improved air stability and electrochemical stability against Li metal compared with Li₇P₃S₁₁ (10.1021/acsami.0c00393). These results do not negate the broader instability concerns, but show that stability is highly chemistry- and interface-dependent.

**Conclusion:** Solid-state electrolytes partially solve lithium-battery safety problems by removing flammable, volatile, leaking liquids, but they introduce or expose other hazards: Li penetration through defects or grain boundaries, critical-current limits, unstable electrode interfaces, and H₂S generation for sulfides. The stability literature is not uniform: some papers emphasize wide voltage windows and improved safety, while sulfide-focused studies report narrow intrinsic windows, moisture sensitivity, and interfacial reactions, with doped or substituted compositions showing partial improvements.

paperclip.answer:
Solid-state electrolytes **do not simply “solve” lithium-battery safety**. The retrieved claims support a more conditional conclusion: they can **reduce some hazards**—for example, nonflammable or flame-retardant polymer/quasi-solid electrolytes are reported for safer lithium-metal or all-solid-state cells—but they also introduce or reveal **new safety-critical failure modes** (10.1039/c9ra08677c; 10.3390/polym12122937; 10.3390/polym13111675).

Key new or remaining hazards include:

- **Toxic gas / air sensitivity in sulfides:** sulfide solid electrolytes can react with atmospheric moisture to generate **H₂S**, causing performance degradation; Sn substitution in Li₆PS₅Cl is presented as a way to improve atmospheric and Li-metal interfacial stability, but the need for such modification underscores the baseline instability problem (10.3390/ma16072751).
- **Thermal runaway is not eliminated:** all-solid-state batteries have been explicitly studied for **blast formation during thermal runaway**, so replacing liquid electrolyte does not make abuse events irrelevant (10.1016/j.isci.2023.108078).
- **Lithium dendrites can still occur in solids:** direct observation of lithium metal dendrites with a ceramic solid electrolyte contradicts the simple idea that a solid electrolyte mechanically blocks dendrites (10.1038/s41598-020-75456-0). Pulse-current protocols also affect dendrite formation/evolution in all-solid-state batteries, indicating dendrite behavior remains an operational safety issue (10.1038/s41467-023-37476-y).
- **Interfaces can be unstable:** Fe-stabilized LLZO shows interface instability versus Li metal, while artificial interfacial layers are reported to improve garnet/Li interfaces—so stability depends strongly on interface engineering, not just the bulk electrolyte (10.1021/acs.jpcc.7b12387; 10.1126/sciadv.1601659).

The main conflicting or nuanced stability results are:

1. **Sulfides are reported as moisture-sensitive, yet some compositions/coatings are called air-stable.** Li₆PS₅Cl-type sulfides are described as moisture-reactive with H₂S generation, while Sn substitution improves atmospheric stability (10.3390/ma16072751). Separately, an oxysulfide nanolayer is reported to make a sulfide electrolyte air-stable and chemically resistant (10.1021/acsomega.0c03453), and Li₃.₆In₇S₁₁.₈Cl is described as an air- and moisture-stable superionic conductor (10.1039/d5sc01907a). This is not necessarily a direct contradiction: it suggests **stability is composition- and surface-dependent**, not intrinsic to all sulfide-like solid electrolytes.

2. **Bulk electrolyte stability and Li-metal interfacial stability are different.** A material may be claimed air/moisture-stable, while separate work emphasizes Li-anode interface instability and the need for stabilization in Li₃InCl₆ and Li₆PS₅Cl systems (10.1016/j.jpowsour.2025.236719). Thus, “stable in air” does not automatically mean “stable against lithium metal.”

3. **Ceramic electrolytes are not guaranteed dendrite-proof.** Chemomechanical design rules are proposed to prevent dendrite formation (10.1038/s41563-020-0655-2), but dendrites have been directly observed with ceramic solid electrolytes (10.1038/s41598-020-75456-0). The nuance is that dendrite suppression appears to require the right material mechanics, interfaces, and cycling protocols, rather than being guaranteed by solidification alone.

Overall: solid-state electrolytes can improve safety in targeted ways, especially flammability, but they also introduce stability, gas-evolution, interface, dendrite, and thermal-runaway concerns that must be engineered around.

edison.answer:
Question: Do solid-state electrolytes solve the safety problems of lithium batteries, or introduce new ones? What conflicting results exist about electrolyte stability?

## Technical synthesis

### 1) What safety problems do solid-state electrolytes target?
Conventional Li-ion batteries (LIBs) rely on volatile, flammable organic liquid electrolytes (OLEs) and porous polyolefin separators, creating well-known hazards: leakage and fire-supporting electrolyte, separator collapse and internal short circuit (ISC), flammable gas evolution, and thermal runaway (TR) driven by a chain of exothermic reactions (SEI decomposition, electrode–electrolyte reactions, cathode oxygen release, etc.). (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 1-3, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 3-6, yu2023batterysafetyfrom pages 1-3)

Solid-state batteries (SSBs) are widely proposed to improve *intrinsic* safety by replacing OLEs with nonvolatile, nonflowable solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) that have higher decomposition temperatures, reduce combustible-gas generation, and (for many ceramics) provide higher mechanical strength that can delay or prevent ISC/dendrite penetration. (yu2023batterysafetyfrom pages 5-8, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 3-6, wu2021progressinthermal pages 1-2)

### 2) Do SSEs “solve” LIB safety problems, or introduce new ones?
**They mitigate important liquid-electrolyte hazards, but do not eliminate TR/ISC risk and can introduce new failure modes.**

**Safety improvements that are reasonably well supported**

- **Lower flammability and less electrolyte-driven combustion energy.** Reviews emphasize that removing volatile OLE reduces direct combustion and can reduce total TR heat release (liquid-electrolyte combustion can be a meaningful fraction of TR energy). (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9)
- **Higher thermal-abuse tolerance in some designs.** Solid electrolytes can delay onset of aggressive chemical reactions and reduce gas-mediated propagation/crosstalk between electrodes, potentially giving higher hot-box temperatures and slower runaway kinetics. (yu2023batterysafetyfrom pages 5-8, yu2023batterysafetyfrom pages 3-5)
- **Some experimental abuse tests show improved outcomes versus LE-LIBs.** A study on sulfide-electrolyte all-solid-state LIBs reports improved resistance to high-temperature electrical shorting, reduced heat generation under heating, stability under overcharge to 5.5 V, and a “fast and effective battery shut-down capability,” avoiding TR upon mechanical damage and air exposure in their test protocols. (liu2023thermalelectricaland pages 1-3)

**Residual and newly introduced hazards (i.e., “new problems”)**

- **Lithium metal can remain the primary fuel even if the electrolyte is nonflammable.** Multiple reviews note Li metal’s low melting point (~180–189 °C) and high reactivity; when molten, Li can greatly accelerate reactions by increasing interfacial contact and diffusion pathways, potentially triggering TR even in SSBs. (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9, han2023incombustiblepolymerelectrolyte pages 4-6)
- **Thermally driven reactions can occur at SSE|Li interfaces.** A calorimetry study shows that some oxide SSEs undergo TR when in contact with metallic Li, driven by oxygen generation from the SSE and subsequent reaction with molten Li; this directly contradicts the simplistic “ceramic electrolyte = safe” assumption. (chen2020thethermalstability pages 1-3)
- **Dendrites/filament penetration and crack-assisted shorting persist.** Reviews emphasize that dendrites can grow within ceramics (oxides, glass-ceramics, crystalline sulfides) and that soft polymer electrolytes cannot reliably suppress dendrites; crack spreading and ISC can generate heat even at room temperature. (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11)
- **Toxic/hazardous byproducts, especially for sulfide SSEs.** Sulfide electrolytes can hydrolyze in humid air to produce **H2S**; this is both a materials-quality issue (impedance rise/conductivity loss) and an occupational safety issue. (yersak2022moisturestabilityof pages 1-2, kreher2023investigatingtheproduction pages 4-5)

Overall, SSEs mainly **remove or reduce** several *liquid-electrolyte-specific* hazards (leakage, volatility, some combustibility and gas evolution), but they **do not inherently prevent** catastrophic failures because (i) interfaces can react, (ii) Li metal and charged cathodes can still drive large exotherms, and (iii) mechanical defects and chemo-mechanical coupling can still create ISCs.

### 3) What conflicting results exist about electrolyte stability?
A recurring conflict is that **electrochemical stability windows can look wide in some experiments, but much narrower under thermodynamic analysis and practical composite-electrode conditions**.

#### 3.1 Apparent wide stability windows vs thermodynamic instability
- **Apparent (often CV-based) windows can be very wide** when measured with semi-blocking electrodes, leading to reports such as ~0–5 V for LGPS and LLZO. (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 1-5)
- **Thermodynamic/DFT calculations predict much narrower decomposition limits.** For example, Han et al. report for LGPS a narrow intrinsic window around **1.71–2.14 V** and for LLZO a stability range around **0.05–2.91 V**, inconsistent with “0–5 V stable” interpretations. (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 8-12, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca)

These differences are attributed to kinetics and test configuration: limited contact area (semi-blocking electrode) can suppress reaction rates and overestimate stability; in composite cathodes/anodes (with carbon and large interfacial area), decomposition is much more likely/accelerated. (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 1-5)

#### 3.2 Kinetic/passivation stabilization vs confirmed decomposition/interphase formation
Even where *practical* stability is observed, it often reflects **passivating interphases or indirect redox mechanisms**, not true thermodynamic stability.

- **Indirect (de)lithiation can widen the observed window.** Nature Materials (2020) demonstrates that argyrodite, garnet, and NASICON SSEs often decompose indirectly via metastable (de)lithiated electrolyte phases, which can make the **observable** stability window notably larger than direct-decomposition predictions, rationalizing some “wider-than-DFT” experimental windows. (schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 22-26, schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 1-6)
- **Yet decomposition still occurs and can be performance-/safety-relevant.** The same work notes that metastable intermediates eventually transform into stable decomposition products that are often poorly conductive (e.g., S/Li2S/LiCl), increasing interfacial resistance. (schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 22-26)

#### 3.3 Example: LLZO oxidation—higher experimental onset than DFT, but not “infinite stability”
- Han et al. show a concrete discrepancy: LLZO’s DFT anodic limit near ~2.91 V, but **CV oxidation onset around ~4.0 V** (interpreted as kinetic overpotential/passivation effects). (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 8-12, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca)
- At the same time, XPS evidence indicates **real chemical changes** (oxygen loss and Zr reduction) beyond the stability limit, undermining the interpretation that the CV window implies complete stability. (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 12-16)

### 4) Safety-relevant stability: moisture stability of sulfide SSEs as a clear “new safety problem”
Unlike OLE flammability, sulfide moisture reactivity creates a distinct hazard category:

- In a “dry room” environment (−40 °C dewpoint), a sulfide SSE powder released **0.1 cc g⁻¹ H2S** in 30 min and its ionic conductivity decreased **>50%**; processing as a slurry (dodecane) reduced H2S release to **0 cc g⁻¹** and conductivity loss to **14%**. (yersak2022moisturestabilityof pages 1-2)
- Occupational health guidance cited for sulfide processing includes **H2S TWA 5 ppm** and **STEL 10 ppm**, underscoring manufacturing-scale safety constraints. (kreher2023investigatingtheproduction pages 4-5)

### 5) Summary table
The following table consolidates how different SSE families trade reduced liquid-electrolyte hazards for new interface/mechanical/toxic-gas risks, and where stability results conflict across methods.

| SSE class / examples | Claimed safety advantages vs liquid electrolyte | New / remaining hazards | Stability controversies / conflicting results | Key quantitative datapoints |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| **Sulfide thiophosphates**: LGPS (Li10GeP2S12), Li6PS5Cl/Li6PS5Br argyrodites, Li7P3S11 | Nonvolatile/nonflowable; generally less flammable than organic liquids; high ionic conductivity and lower heat generation can improve abuse tolerance; some sulfide ASSB cells showed better resistance to high-temperature electrical shorting, overcharge tolerance, and shutdown behavior after damage/air exposure than liquid-electrolyte LIBs (yu2023batterysafetyfrom pages 5-8, wu2021progressinthermal pages 1-2, liu2023thermalelectricaland pages 1-3) | Moisture sensitivity with **toxic H2S** release; can also form SO2 under decomposition/oxidation; hydrolysis products increase interfacial impedance and cut conductivity; dendrite/filament penetration and grain-boundary shorting still occur; interfaces with charged cathodes or Li can generate Joule heat and exotherms; molten Li and full-charge cathode oxygen release can intensify failure (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11, luo2024safetyconcernsin pages 7-9, yersak2022moisturestabilityof pages 1-2, kreher2023investigatingtheproduction pages 4-5) | Classic conflict: semi-blocking-electrode CV often suggested very wide windows, but DFT and practical composite-electrode tests show narrow intrinsic windows and real redox/decomposition. For LGPS, narrow thermodynamic window is consistent with sulfide instability; argyrodites can show wider **apparent** windows because of kinetic barriers or indirect metastable (de)lithiation, yet still decompose to Li2S/S/LiCl/P-containing products and raise impedance (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 12-16, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 1-5, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 16-19, schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 22-26, schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 1-6, schwietert2021firstprinciplespredictionof pages 1-2) | **LGPS DFT window ~1.71–2.14 V** (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 8-12, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca); at **−40 °C dew point**, a sulfide powder [(Li2S)75(P2S5)25 + 20 mol% LiI] released **0.1 cc g⁻¹ H2S** after 30 min and lost **>50%** conductivity, while slurry processing cut H2S to **0 cc g⁻¹** and conductivity drop to **14%** (yersak2022moisturestabilityof pages 1-2); reported occupational limits for H2S: **5 ppm TWA**, **10 ppm STEL** (kreher2023investigatingtheproduction pages 4-5); shorting in one charged sulfide system reported at **275.5 °C** (luo2024safetyconcernsin pages 7-9) |
| **Oxide garnets**: LLZO and doped LLZO | Nonflammable, high thermal stability, high modulus, can delay internal shorting and avoid leakage/spitting fire; often regarded as among the safest inorganic SSE families and sometimes stable with Li at room temperature because of passivating surface products/interphases (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 3-6, wu2021progressinthermal pages 1-2, schwietert2021firstprinciplespredictionof pages 4-5) | Not intrinsically immune to Li-related failure: dendrite/filament penetration and crack-assisted shorting still reported; some oxide SSEs react strongly with Li, especially at elevated temperature or with molten Li; oxygen release from certain oxide SSEs in contact with Li can trigger highly exothermic reactions and thermal runaway (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9, chen2020thethermalstability pages 1-3) | Major conflict between thermodynamics and experiment: DFT predicts LLZO is not stable across 0–5 V and can oxidize/reduce outside a narrower window, while CV often shows much wider apparent stability because kinetics/passivation mask decomposition. Yet spectroscopy confirms real oxidation/reduction: O loss on charging and reduced Zr states; practical oxidation onset is higher than DFT but not infinite stability (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 12-16, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 8-12, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 1-5, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 16-19, schwietert2021firstprinciplespredictionof pages 1-2, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca) | **LLZO DFT window ~0.05–2.91 V** (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 8-12, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca); experimental **CV oxidation onset ~4.0 V** (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof pages 8-12, han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca); ARC study found garnet was the oxide tested with **no obvious heat release with Li**, unlike several other oxide SSEs (chen2020thethermalstability pages 1-3) |
| **NASICON-type oxides**: LATP, LAGP | Nonflammable, thermally robust, mechanically stronger than polymers/liquids; can suppress leakage and improve abuse tolerance versus liquid electrolytes (wu2021progressinthermal pages 1-2, luo2024safetyconcernsin pages 1-2) | Reduced by Li to mixed-conducting interphases; interfacial resistance rises during cycling; can undergo fierce thermal behavior when paired with Li under some conditions; contact evolution during Li plating/stripping creates local hotspots and instability (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9, luo2024safetyconcernsin pages 5-6) | Another strong stability conflict: practical measurements sometimes show partially reversible or kinetically stabilized behavior, but DFT/advanced modeling and spectroscopy indicate reduction against Li and decomposition/interphase growth. Nature Materials 2020 argues indirect (de)lithiation can widen observed windows relative to direct-decomposition predictions, yet decomposition still follows (schwietert2021firstprinciplespredictionof pages 4-5, schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 22-26, schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 1-6) | **LAGP reduction predicted ~2.31 V** by indirect-path analysis vs **2.70 V** by direct-decomposition approach; experiment shows reduction peak near **2.4 V** (schwietert2020clarifyingtherelationship pages 22-26); review notes some high-valence NASICON SSEs form unstable **mixed-conductive interphases** with Li (luo2024safetyconcernsin pages 5-6) |
| **Polymer electrolytes**: PEO-based SPEs, flame-retardant polymers | Solid, nonleaking, often less flammable than liquid electrolytes under normal use; can reduce external combustion and leakage; chemistry can be tuned with flame retardants/incombustible groups (han2023incombustiblepolymerelectrolyte pages 4-6) | Soft mechanics mean poor dendrite suppression; polymers can still decompose, char, shrink, or burn under flame/high temperature; Li metal remains a major hazard if the cell is breached; cathode oxygen release can dominate thermal runaway heat (han2023incombustiblepolymerelectrolyte pages 4-6, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11) | Practical “solid-state = safe” claim is especially contested here: polymer cells may have higher self-heating onset than liquid cells, but PEO-based and composite polymer systems can still combust or fail if Li dendrites short the cell. Electrochemical stability also depends strongly on salt and morphology, so computed polymer-matrix windows do not guarantee full-electrolyte stability (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9, han2023incombustiblepolymerelectrolyte pages 4-6) | PEO pyrolysis/decomposition reported around **~400 °C** (han2023incombustiblepolymerelectrolyte pages 4-6); Li metal melts at **180.5–189 °C** and can burn rapidly when molten/air-exposed (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11, han2023incombustiblepolymerelectrolyte pages 4-6); one review reports SS-LMB self-heating onset around **~250 °C** for SPE cells vs **90–110 °C** for OLE cells, and total heat release often **< half** of OLE-LMBs (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9) |
| **Composite / hybrid SSEs**: polymer–ceramic composites, mixed solid electrolytes | Can combine ceramic nonflammability/mechanical strength with polymer processability and better interfacial contact; often proposed to improve abuse tolerance and mitigate brittle fracture or poor contact in pure ceramics (wu2021progressinthermal pages 1-2, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 3-6) | Inherit failure modes from both parents: polymer fraction can still char/burn; ceramic fraction can crack; heterogeneous interfaces create local current constriction, contact loss, and filament initiation; some hybrid cells still show obvious combustion or thermally driven failure when Li/interphase chemistry is unfavorable (luo2024safetyconcernsin pages 1-2, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 3-6, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9, zhao2023advancedsolidstatelithium pages 3-4) | Stability is highly system-specific: improved apparent cycling can come from kinetic/passivating interphases rather than true thermodynamic compatibility. *Table: This table compares the main solid-state electrolyte families on claimed safety gains, newly introduced hazards, and the major disagreements in the literature about electrochemical stability. It is useful for answering whether solid electrolytes solve lithium-battery safety issues or mainly shift them into new chemical, interfacial, and mechanical failure modes.*

### 6) Bottom line
SSEs do **not** “solve” battery safety in a universal sense. They **can** reduce key hazards associated with volatile OLEs (leakage, flammability, some TR propagation mechanisms) and can improve certain abuse responses in specific cell designs. (yu2023batterysafetyfrom pages 5-8, liu2023thermalelectricaland pages 1-3, wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 6-9)

However, they can also **introduce new safety problems** (e.g., H2S generation for sulfides, moisture sensitivity, manufacturing dry-room constraints) and **do not eliminate** fundamental failure triggers (Li-metal reactivity at high temperature, interfacial decomposition that increases resistance/Joule heating, and dendrite/filament penetration aided by cracks and defects). (wang2023safetyperceptionsof pages 9-11, chen2020thethermalstability pages 1-3, yersak2022moisturestabilityof pages 1-2, kreher2023investigatingtheproduction pages 4-5)

### Visual evidence for stability conflicts
Han et al. provide figures showing DFT-predicted stability windows for LGPS and LLZO and an LLZO CV showing higher oxidation onset (~4 V), illustrating the common DFT–experiment discrepancy in SSE stability interpretation. (han2016electrochemicalstabilityof media 1f6e2bca)

### Safety and Stability of Solid-State Electrolytes in Lithium Batteries

**Introduction.** Traditional lithium-ion batteries use flammable organic liquid electrolytes, which pose risks of thermal runaway, leakage, and combustion. Solid-state electrolytes (SSEs) have emerged as a transformative solution, promising to mitigate these hazards while enabling lithium-metal anodes.

**Problems Solved by SSEs.** Thermal stability and non-flammability: SSEs (particularly oxides and halides) are generally non-flammable and can prevent the chain reactions leading to thermal runaway. Leakage prevention: as solids, they eliminate the risk of flammable electrolyte leakage. Mechanical suppression: robust mechanical properties are designed to physically suppress lithium dendrite penetration.

**New Problems Introduced.** Dendrite formation within solids: contrary to early expectations, lithium filaments can still grow through SSEs along grain boundaries or pores, often driven by the electrolyte's electronic conductivity. Interface/interphase reactions: solid-solid contact is prone to chemical and electrochemical instability, forming resistive interphases that cause capacity fade. Gas evolution hazards: sulfide SSEs (argyrodites) react with moisture to release toxic H2S, and charged cathode–SSE reactions can trigger oxygen release. Mechanical failure: volume changes cause cracking and voids, leading to "soft shorts" that require high stack pressure.

**Conflicting Results in Electrolyte Stability.** Thermodynamic vs. kinetic stability: theory predicts narrow stability windows for most SSEs (especially sulfides), yet experiments show apparently wide windows because decomposition is kinetically slow or forms a passivating interphase. Composition and doping: studies on LLZO garnet show conflicting results on the best dopants (Al, Ga, Ta); some find improved stability against Li metal, others report increased electronic conductivity that promotes dendrites. Interface characterization: different techniques (EIS, SEM, XPS) yield varying results on SEI nature and thickness, leading to conflicting models.

**Conclusion.** SSEs are a major leap in safety by eliminating flammable liquids, but they are not a "silver bullet"; they replace liquid-based risks with new challenges of internal lithium filament growth, interfacial reactivity, and mechanical degradation.

question: Do smaller nanoparticles always have higher catalytic activity? What contradictory findings exist about the nanoparticle size effect in catalysis?

alone.answer:
No. **Smaller nanoparticles do not always have higher catalytic activity**—they usually have higher **metal dispersion** (more surface atoms per gram), but the **intrinsic activity per surface atom/TOF** can increase, decrease, be size-independent, or show an optimum.

Key reason: catalysis depends on the **type of site** exposed—terraces, edges, corners, metal–support perimeter sites, oxidation state, and required atom ensembles—not just total surface area.

### Contradictory size-effect findings

| System | Reported size effect | Conditions / details | Takeaway |
|---|---:|---|---|
| **Au/TiO₂, CO oxidation** | Small Au is much more active, but not monotonically “smaller is better” | Haruta showed Au particles of a few nm oxidize CO even below room temperature; large Au is nearly inactive. Later work found activity depends strongly on Au/TiO₂ perimeter and cluster geometry. | Classic case supporting “small is active,” but optimum often ~2–5 nm rather than the smallest possible. DOI: **10.1246/cl.1987.405**; Science size-selected Au/TiO₂: **10.1126/science.281.5383.1647** |
| **Co/CNF, Fischer–Tropsch synthesis** | **Smaller Co particles became less active** below ~6 nm | Co particles ~2.6–27 nm on carbon nanofibers; ~220 °C, ~35 bar, H₂/CO ≈ 2. TOF roughly constant for 6–27 nm but dropped sharply below ~6 nm; methane selectivity increased for smaller particles. | CO dissociation needs suitable Co ensembles; very small particles are more oxidized/strongly bound to support and less intrinsically active. DOI: **10.1021/ja058282w** |
| **Pt/C, oxygen reduction reaction ORR** | **Specific activity often increases with Pt particle size** | Acid electrolyte, RDE/fuel-cell-relevant ORR, typically evaluated at 0.9 V vs RHE. Small Pt particles bind O/OH too strongly; larger particles expose more Pt(111)-like terrace sites. Mass activity can show an optimum around ~2–4 nm because dispersion decreases at large size. | Contradicts “smaller = better”: per surface Pt atom, larger particles can be more active. DOI example: **10.1038/nmat3458** |
| **Ru, ammonia synthesis / N₂ activation** | Very small Ru clusters can be less active | N₂ dissociation requires step/B5-type ensembles; promoted Ru catalysts often show optimum particle sizes rather than monotonic increase with decreasing size. Typical NH₃ synthesis: 350–450 °C, elevated H₂/N₂ pressure. | If the reaction needs multi-atom ensembles, ultrasmall particles may lack the right sites. Mechanistic step-site evidence: **10.1103/PhysRevLett.83.1814**; theory: **10.1126/science.1106435** |
| **Structure-insensitive hydrogenations, e.g. ethylene hydrogenation on Pt/Pd/Ni** | TOF can be nearly size-independent over a moderate size range | Mild gas-phase hydrogenation conditions; once particles are large enough to behave metallically, terrace/edge differences may matter little. | Smaller particles give higher rate per gram because of dispersion, but not necessarily higher TOF. |
| **Pd/Au/Pt selective hydrogenations or oxidations** | Size trends can reverse depending on selectivity target | For alkyne hydrogenation, alcohol oxidation, or CO oxidation, small particles may be more active but less selective, or activity may correlate with oxidized/perimeter sites rather than size alone. | Apparent “size effect” may actually be oxidation-state, support, or ensemble-size effect. |

### Why the literature can look contradictory

1. **Mass activity vs TOF are different.**  
   Smaller particles usually give more exposed metal atoms per gram, so rate per gram may rise, while **TOF per exposed atom** may fall.

2. **Different reactions require different sites.**  
   - CO oxidation on Au often benefits from small particles and metal–support perimeter sites.  
   - Fischer–Tropsch and ammonia synthesis need larger ensembles/steps, so ultrasmall particles can be worse.

3. **Binding-energy volcano effects.**  
   Very small particles often bind intermediates too strongly, causing CO/OH/H poisoning; larger particles may bind too weakly. The optimum is often intermediate.

4. **Support and pretreatment matter.**  
   A 2 nm Pt particle on carbon is not equivalent to 2 nm Pt on TiO₂, CeO₂, Al₂O₃, etc.; charge transfer, SMSI, oxidation state, and perimeter sites change the trend.

5. **Ultrasmall clusters are not just “small crystals.”**  
   Below ~1–2 nm, quantum/electronic effects, fluxionality, and nonmetallic behavior can dominate.

### Bottom line

**Smaller nanoparticles often have higher apparent activity per mass because of higher surface area, but they do not always have higher intrinsic catalytic activity.** Depending on the reaction, catalyst, support, and metric used, the size effect can be:

- monotonic smaller-is-better,
- larger-is-better,
- volcano-shaped with an optimum,
- or nearly size-independent.

unified.answer:
No. The evidence does **not** support a universal rule that smaller nanoparticles always have higher catalytic activity. Size effects are real, but they can be **positive, negative, reaction-specific, support-dependent, and metric-dependent**.

- **Cases where smaller particles are more active:**  
  Smaller Pt nanoparticles showed higher TOF: 2.5 nm Pt gave 2.08 e site⁻¹ s⁻¹, decreasing to 0.13 e site⁻¹ s⁻¹ at 4.5 nm (10.1021/jacsau.1c00074). For Ru-catalyzed biomass valorisation, furan formation TOF dropped sharply from 98 h⁻¹ over 2.3 nm Ru to 1 h⁻¹ over 24 nm Ru (10.1039/d0cs00130a). Smaller Pd nanoparticles were reported to expose more reactive Pd dimers, increasing intrinsic catalytic activity (10.1021/acsnano.4c04193). Reviews also report larger noble-metal nanoparticles requiring higher temperatures for total CO conversion because of lower activity (10.1039/C9TA00074G).

- **Contradictory cases where larger particles are more active:**  
  In Fischer–Tropsch synthesis over cobalt, enlarging cobalt crystallites slightly increased CO conversion from 77.0 to 80.6% and markedly increased TOF from 3.9 × 10⁻² to 6.4 × 10⁻² s⁻¹ (10.1038/s41467-018-05755-8). Separately, Fischer–Tropsch microkinetic analysis reports that CO consumption TOF per exposed surface metal atom decreases steeply when particle size becomes less than 6 nm (10.1039/c3cp52506f). Thus, for Co FTS, “smaller is better” is directly contradicted.

- **Reaction-specific size effects can even occur on the same metal:**  
  For Ru nanoparticles, furan formation was strongly favored by small particles, but carbonyl hydrogenation TOF changed only from 237 to 307 h⁻¹ when size increased from 2.3 to 24 nm—i.e., nearly insensitive or slightly higher for larger particles (10.1039/d0cs00130a). This shows that size effects depend on the reaction pathway, not just on particle size.

- **Activity metric matters:**  
  Smaller Pt particles can give higher electrochemical surface area and mass activity, but also lower durability than larger Pt particles (10.1016/j.adapen.2021.100071). Because apparent activity can reflect surface area rather than intrinsic site activity, TOF normalized per active site is recommended for fair comparison (10.1021/acsnano.8b07700).

- **Mechanistic nuance:**  
  Size changes can alter phase, surface structure, support interactions, and dynamic restructuring. For cobalt, particles below 20 nm are typically FCC while those above 40 nm are HCP (10.1021/acs.chemrev.2c00508). Supported Au shows size-dependent metal–support/adsorbate–particle interactions under CO oxidation conditions (10.1038/s41467-020-19484-4; 10.1073/pnas.1800262115). Metal nanoparticles can also restructure under reaction conditions (10.1016/J.NANTOD.2018.04.005).

**Bottom line:** smaller nanoparticles often improve surface-area-based activity, but they do **not** always have higher intrinsic catalytic activity. The contradictory findings—especially Co Fischer–Tropsch and reaction-dependent Ru behavior—show that nanoparticle size effects are catalyst- and reaction-specific rather than universally monotonic.

paperclip.answer:
No. The retrieved evidence does **not** support the rule that “smaller nanoparticles always have higher catalytic activity.” It supports a more nuanced view: nanoparticle size can matter, but activity/selectivity also depends on geometry, composition, nanostructure, support/interface, active-site identity, and even structural changes under reaction conditions.

Key contradictory or qualifying findings:

- **Smaller size is often attractive because of high surface area**, and metal nanoparticles are broadly described as catalytically active partly due to “high surface area” and tunable morphologies (10.3390/ma12213602). This is the basis for the common intuition that smaller particles should be more active.

- **But size effects are not necessarily monotonic.** Atomically precise Au nanoclusters are highlighted as enabling size–activity studies at the atomic level because conventional polydisperse nanoparticles obscure size/structure/property relations; this implies that “size” alone is not a simple universal predictor (10.1021/prechem.3c00008).

- **Different reactions can show different size dependencies.** For cobalt particles in CO dissociation, the literature frames the issue as a need to enumerate active sites to understand size dependence, indicating that activity is tied to the number/type of active sites rather than simply smaller particle diameter (10.1021/acscatal.1c00651).

- **Selectivity can change with particle size, not just activity.** Pd/Al₂O₃ catalysts show particle-size-dependent selectivity in 1-butene isomerization versus hydrogenation, so “better” catalysis depends on the desired product, not merely higher rate (10.1038/s41467-021-26411-8).

- **Bimetallic systems add further complexity.** A “conjugated dual size effect” in core–shell particles was reported to synergize bimetallic catalysis, meaning both core/shell size relationships and composition can govern performance rather than a single smaller-is-better trend (10.1038/s41467-023-36147-2). Similarly, Au–Pd catalysts show dependence on size, nanostructure, and composition for benzyl alcohol oxidation (10.1016/j.jcat.2019.05.002).

- **Electronic/structural state can override simple size arguments.** Distinct gold species contribute differently to CO oxidation reactivity, so the catalytically relevant factor may be which Au species is present, not just nanoparticle diameter (10.1038/ncomms13481). Pretreatments and modifiers can strongly affect the electronic states of ~1 nm Au particles, further complicating any direct size–activity rule (10.3390/molecules21040432).

- **Catalysts can restructure under reaction conditions.** Rh catalysts undergo structural changes during CO oxidation that impact kinetics, showing that the “size effect” measured before reaction may not be the operative descriptor during catalysis (10.1021/jacsau.2c00595).

**Bottom line:** smaller nanoparticles often provide more surface area, but the evidence set shows multiple contradictions to a universal smaller-is-more-active rule: size effects can be reaction-specific, nonmonotonic, selectivity-changing, composition-dependent, geometry-dependent, and dynamically altered under reaction conditions.

Nanoparticle size is an important control knob for catalysis, but **smaller nanoparticles do not always have higher catalytic activity**. The literature contains clear counterexamples in which activity is **nonmonotonic (an optimum size exists), reversed (larger particles are intrinsically more active on a per-site basis), or effectively size-independent over a size window**, depending on reaction, support, environment, and how activity is normalized (mass vs surface area vs TOF). *Table: This table summarizes representative cases where nanoparticle catalytic activity does not simply increase as size decreases. It highlights nonmonotonic optima, larger-more-active behavior, and size-independent regimes across Au, Pt, and Pd catalysts.*

## Contradictory findings about the “smaller = more active” rule

### 1) **Nonmonotonic size–activity trends (activity maxima / volcano behavior)**
* **Au-catalyzed CO oxidation:** A prominent example is supported Au where activity can be **highly peaked around ~3 nm**, and **decreases steeply below ~3 nm** rather than increasing further. This behavior can differ with support (e.g., titania vs carbon) and has been interpreted as a superposition of an “intrinsic” small-particle deactivation with a titania-induced activation that creates a maximum. (hayden2007cooxidationon pages 5-6)
* **Size-selected Au clusters:** Model Aun/TiO2 catalysts show **strong, cluster-by-cluster variation** with **significant activity appearing already at Au3**, emphasizing that “smaller” does not imply a smooth trend—specific atomicities can be special. (lee2005clustersizeeffects pages 1-3)
* **Theory for Au clusters:** Microkinetic/DFT analyses predict **distinct optimum sizes** depending on whether the cluster is planar (<14 atoms) or 3D, with optima reported at **Au9 (planar)** and **Au79 (3D)**—again, explicitly **nonmonotonic** and not “always smaller is better”. (liu2018optimumparticlesize pages 1-4)

### 2) **Reversed trends (larger nanoparticles more active per surface site)**
* **Pt ORR (electrocatalysis):** Multiple studies summarized in mass-selected Pt nanoparticle work report that **ORR specific activity increases with increasing Pt particle size**, commonly rationalized by the higher fraction of terrace-like sites on larger particles and by overly strong binding of oxygenated intermediates at undercoordinated sites prevalent on small nanoparticles. (perez‐alonso2012theeffectof pages 1-2)
* **Pd selective hydrogenation:** For **1-hexyne hydrogenation**, TOF per Pd surface atom was reported to increase by **~an order of magnitude** when particle size grows from **6–11 nm** to **~13–14 nm** (e.g., ~0.5 s−1 to ~6.6–9.2 s−1), directly contradicting a generic expectation that smaller particles are intrinsically more active. (semagina2007palladiumnanoparticlesize pages 2-3)

### 3) **Size-independent regimes (weak or negligible size effect over a window)**
* **Pt ORR below ~5 nm:** Some experiments report **size-independent ORR activity for Pt nanoparticles below ~5 nm**, attributing this to similar surface compositions/electronic structures or terrace-site dominance in that range; other authors note that once support-related artefacts are corrected, a size effect may disappear in the sub-5 nm regime. (sheng2011sizeinfluenceon pages 5-7, perez‐alonso2012theeffectof pages 1-2)

### 4) **Apparent size effects can be confounded or even spurious**
* For Au CO oxidation and PROX, critical reviews note that some “size effects” may be entangled with **gold loading, synthesis-dependent dispersion, and accessible gold surface area**; plotting activity metrics against gold content/surface area can change the interpretation. (kipnis2014goldinco pages 5-7)

## Why smaller nanoparticles are not guaranteed to be more active
1. **Normalization matters:** Mass activity may peak at an intermediate size because decreasing size increases surface area but can decrease intrinsic per-site activity; this trade-off produces optima (e.g., ORR mass activity maxima near a few nm). (nesselberger2011theparticlesize pages 1-2, tritsaris2011atomicscalemodelingof pages 1-2)
2. **Structure sensitivity and site distribution:** Size changes the fraction of terraces, edges, and corners. Undercoordinated sites can be either beneficial or detrimental depending on the reaction and on spectator adsorption (electrolyte/adsorbates). (perez‐alonso2012theeffectof pages 1-2, nesselberger2011theparticlesize pages 1-2)
3. **Adsorption energetics / Sabatier optima:** Size-driven changes to CO/O2 binding (Au CO oxidation) can yield intermediate-binding “best” sizes rather than monotonic scaling. (liu2018optimumparticlesize pages 1-4)
4. **Support/interface effects:** For supported Au, the support can induce activation that competes with intrinsic small-particle deactivation, giving support-dependent optima and even opposite trends on different supports. (hayden2007cooxidationon pages 5-6)

## Visual evidence for nonmonotonic performance relationships
Although not strictly a size plot, nanoparticle electrocatalysis literature commonly shows **volcano-like (nonmonotonic) performance correlations**. For example, Strasser’s account includes a volcano-like activity dependence on composition for nanoparticle OER catalysts (illustrating the general principle of peaked performance landscapes rather than monotonic scaling). (strasser2016freeelectronsto media 57edfd71)

## Conclusion
Across heterogeneous catalysis and electrocatalysis, **smaller nanoparticles do not always have higher catalytic activity**. Contradictory findings include: (i) **nonmonotonic “optimum size” behavior** in Au CO oxidation and in ORR mass activity, (ii) **larger-more-active specific activity/TOF** in Pt ORR and Pd hydrogenation, and (iii) **size-independent windows** (e.g., Pt ORR reported below ~5 nm under certain conditions). These contradictions arise because size changes not only surface area but also surface structure, adsorption energetics, support interactions, and even the validity of the measured “size effect” if confounders are not controlled. (hayden2007cooxidationon pages 5-6, liu2018optimumparticlesize pages 1-4, perez‐alonso2012theeffectof pages 1-2, sheng2011sizeinfluenceon pages 5-7, semagina2007palladiumnanoparticlesize pages 2-3)

### The Nanoparticle Size Effect in Catalysis—Is Smaller Always Better?

**1. Introduction.** A foundational axiom in catalysis has been that reducing nanoparticle size increases catalytic activity, attributed to the geometric expansion of the surface-to-volume ratio and a higher density of active sites. However, at atomic-level precision, empirical evidence frequently confounds this simple linear relationship: smaller particles do not always exhibit higher activity, and a "scaling paradox" exists where activity peaks at an optimal size or even decreases with further reduction.

**2. Why Smaller Is Often (But Not Always) Better.** Geometric effects: small nanoparticles have a high proportion of low-coordinated surface atoms at edges, corners, and defects that are more reactive. Electronic effects: below ~5 nm (fewer than ~10,000 atoms), particles enter the quantum size effect regime where continuous bands transition into discrete levels, altering bonding energies.

**3. Contradictory Findings: The "Optimal Size" Phenomenon.** (A) Ammonia synthesis argues for larger particles: on iron, the rate-determining N2 dissociation requires C7 sites hard to stabilize on small clusters, so TOF increases with particle size, peaking >10 nm; cobalt has an optimal 20–30 nm because the active hcp phase appears only at intermediate sizes. (B) Gold: inert in bulk but active for CO oxidation below 5 nm, peaking near 2.1 nm and dropping below that due to loss of metallic character; ultrasmall clusters form dynamic low-coordinated atoms (DLCAs) as true active sites. (C) CO2 methanation on nickel: optimal ~2.5 nm, with smaller particles suffering surface poisoning from too-tightly-bound intermediates. (D) Palladium: benzyl alcohol oxidation peaks at 4 nm, with smaller particles over-binding reactants due to Fermi-level shifts.

**4. Apparent vs. Real Structure Insensitivity.** Some reactions show constant TOF regardless of size, but operando studies suggest rapid restructuring; e.g., in ethene hydrogenation over nickel, larger particles rearrange to match optimal configurations, yielding "apparent structure insensitivity."

**5. Conclusion.** The assumption that smaller nanoparticles always provide higher activity is a simplification. The optimal size is reaction-specific and balances maximizing active sites against over-binding, surface poisoning, or loss of ensemble sites.
